executive_summary: The dominant thread running through today's content is institutional resilience under pressure — the capacity of established systems to respond to sudden, destabilizing threats. The most concrete expression of this is the breaking news of a gunman being shot and killed near the White House by Secret Service agents, a stark reminder that the security architecture protecting the executive branch remains in active, lethal deployment. This incident connects directly to the Foreign Affairs newsletter on Ebola's lessons, which interrogates how institutions learn — or fail to learn — from acute crises, drawing a clear line between public health emergency response and security preparedness as parallel tests of systemic readiness. Both stories ultimately ask the same question: when a threat materializes without warning, how well do the protocols, people, and institutions designed to contain it actually hold? Today's news cycle, sparse on long-form analysis, places that question in sharp relief with real-world evidence rather than theoretical framing.

items.headline: Stephen and I
items.blurb: Stephen Colbert went off the air last week. Today, a Morning writer reflects on the late-night host's ability to find connection, recounting a personal moment from a 2007 taping of 'The Colbert Report' and what made Colbert special to so many audiences over two decades.

items.headline: In his own words
items.blurb: Colbert's 'Late Show' found its identity in needling President Trump. CBS says that's not why it canceled the series — late-night interview shows are expensive to make, and viewership has fallen over the decades. Colbert sat down with a colleague to talk about the motivations behind the cancellation, explaining how authoritarians don't like comedians and discussing how he evolved the show and what he might do next.

items.headline: The end of an institution
items.blurb: Comedy critic Jason Zinoman looked back on the 33-year run of 'The Late Show,' which began after David Letterman was passed up for the 'Tonight Show' job and decided to compete against it instead. Both Letterman and Colbert came into the show as ironic outsiders, and both sanded down those personalities a bit in their turn to the mainstream — but not entirely.

items.headline: Making sense of an Alcaraz-less French Open
items.blurb: The French Open will not come down to Carlos Alcaraz and Jannik Sinner. At least probably not, given that the tournament starts today at Roland Garros and Alcaraz is not in the draw because of a dreaded wrist injury. Without the two-time defending champion, there's a clear lane for his chief rival. The 24-year-old Sinner will complete the career Grand Slam if he takes care of business against a weakened field. The women's draw is a lot more open, with Iga Świątek and Aryna Sabalenka entering as roughly co-favorites.

items.headline: Knicks-Cavs is looking sweepy
items.blurb: The Knicks are on the verge of their first NBA Finals in 27 years after a 121-108 Game 3 victory in Cleveland, where home support and a certain famous couple didn't make the Cavs seem any less shell-shocked from their Game 1 collapse. Here's your regular reminder that no NBA team has ever blown a 3-0 lead.

breaking_digest.narrative:
Secret Service agents shot and killed a gunman near the White House on Saturday, according to officials [1]. The incident marked a serious security breach in the vicinity of the executive mansion, though no further details on the shooter's identity or motive were immediately available. The Secret Service responded to the threat and neutralized the suspect.

Separately, the Cannes Film Festival concluded its 2026 edition with the Palme d'Or, the festival's top prize, awarded to 'Fjord' [2]. The announcement capped the prestigious international film competition held on the French Riviera.

references.title: Gunman in shooting near White House is killed by Secret Service, officials say
